newsitem.title: USA: Mexico Aztec redemption sparks Brady call concerns.
newsitem.headline: Mexico Aztec redemption sparks Brady call concerns.

text.p: The early redemption of Aztec bonds announced by Mexico on Tuesday highlights the hitherto neglected call risks in Brady bonds, analysts said.

Until now, market players have treated the call provision of Brady bonds as a theoretical possibility with no real price impact. But early redemption of the Aztec on the heels of last year's roaring rally could prompt number crunchers to take a fresh look at some likely call candidates, analysts said.
"People will begin to look at the upside for some Bradies," said James Barrineau, Latin American fixed income analyst at Smith Barney.
All Brady bonds are callable at par.

Aztec, issued in 1988, was a precursor to the Brady-type of restructured debt a year later. It is 47.2 percent collateralized with U.S. Treasury securities and has the high current coupon of 7.40 percent.
Aztec traded above par after the Mexcian government announcement, then slipped to par with slumping U.S. Treasuries during Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to Congress.

Dan Peirce, Brady debt strategist at Bank of Boston, said short-term investors were attracted by Aztec's high coupon, which, before the March 27 redemption, the bond could bring an extra 15 basis points of return.
Gary Evans, emerging market debt strategist at Lehman Brothers stressed the Aztec is unique among emerging market debt.
The Aztec bond has been trading 1-5/8 points over LIBOR, almost twice the spread of the other Brady floaters, he noted.
Evans did not see a rash of redemptions.
"I just don't think that will happen," he said, adding: "Not many are trading close to par."
Peirce agreed that risk of early redemption of Brady bonds is not high.

Discount bonds, many of which are trading close to 100, are more likely than par bonds to be redeemed, he said. But unless U.S. interest rates fall dramatically, it would not make sense for indebted countries to redeem them, Peirce said.
A few candidates for early redemption are Poland discounts, which was bid 98.00, and various Philippine floaters.

Poland's long-term foreign currency debt is rated BBB by Standard and Poor's and Baa3 by Moody's Investors Service. The Philippines is rated BB and Ba2. Moody's said last month that it was reviewing the Philippine rating for possible upgrade.
The signficance of Aztec redemption lies in the $400 million of the collateral Mexico could free up and some $80 million in cost savings, said Smith Barney's Barrineau.
"It it is another occasion that Mexico is doing a great job on debt management," he said. "It is sending a positive signal to the market."
The Mexican government said it had retired about $1.5 billion of the bonds between 1992 and 1996, leaving $1.06 billion to be redeemed.n
Traders said while the call premium would not be priced in Brady bonds any time soon, it may nudge more investors towards the noncallable global bonds.
"It's pure sovereign risk," said a trader with a U.S. investment house.
UMS 26, launched last year to buy back Bradies, has been a top performer since it was freed to trade on secondary market. At 1500 EST/2000 GMT, It was quoted 113-1/2 bid, down 1-7/8 on the day.
Other UMS bonds were also all trading above par, he said.
